CMLIT 1: CMLIT 1 provides a survey of Western literary tradition and considers a variety of genres -- such as epic, drama, sonnet, essay, saga, chronicle, folktale, and novel -- with attention to the literary and historical contexts which these works reflect in the Ancient, Medieval, and Renaissance (Early Modern) periods.
CMLIT 3: Comparative analysis of drama, essay, novel, poetry, and stories from traditional oral forms to contemporary expressions of African literary styles.
CMLIT 4: Satisfies General Education (GH), International Cultures (IL), Other Cultures (BA) requirements.
CMLIT 5: Comparative interpretation of the oral and written literary traditions of North, Central, and South America.
CMLIT 6: This course serves as an introduction to philosophy through the critical and analytic reading of popular, classic, and insightful literature - novels, plays, poetry, and creative non-fiction - from both Western and Non-western authors and cultures.
CMLIT 7: This course provides an introduction to the diverse literatures of the region known as the Middle East.
CMLIT 10: The development of literature around the world - from epic, legend, lyric, etc. in the oral tradition to modern written forms.
CMLIT 10U: The development of literature around the world--from epic, legend, lyric, etc. in the oral tradition to modern written forms.
CMLIT 11: The figure of the hero/heroine examined in world literature as a vehicle for expressing social and cultural values.
CMLIT 12: The power, ethics, and excitement of drama and related forms of performance literature, presented in a global and comparative context.
CMLIT 13: Virtual worlds from anicent to postmodern, in a comparative and global context that includes literature, film, and online multiplayer games.
CMLIT 19N: "Being in the Universe" considers three fundamental questions of human existence from both humanistic and scientific perspectives: (1) What is the nature of our universe, and to what extent are creatures like ourselves a predictable consequence of it?
CMLIT 20: This course takes you on a historical walk across space and time, as we seek to answer one of humanity's most enduring questions: What is the Good Life?
CMLIT 83S: International topics in literature and culture; each seminar will have a specific topic as announced (see the Comparative Literature Web site).
CMLIT 97: Formal courses given infrequently to explore, in depth, a comparatively narrow subject which may be topical or of special interest.
CMLIT 99: Courses offered in foreign countries by individual or group instruction.
CMLIT 100: CMLIT 100 Reading Across Cultures, is an introductory course to the discipline of Comparative Literature.

CMLIT 105: Literary humor expressed as satire, comedy, and farce--from ancient times to the present--in an international and multicultural context.
CMLIT 106: The growth and development of the legend of King Arthur, from medieval Europe to modern Japan.

CMLIT 108: World mythology: myths primarily of non-Western cultures, based on selected areas and traditions around the world.
CMLIT 109: Myths, legends, and literatures of Native American cultures.

CMLIT 112N: Introduction to Global Drama, Theater, and Performance will enable students to discover the power and excitement of drama in a global context.
CMLIT 113: Comparative study of diverse interpretations of stories from the Bible in Judaism and Christianity.
CMLIT 120: Important literary works dealing with witchcraft, demonology, vampirism, ghosts, and related concepts, from biblical times to present.
CMLIT 122: A study of the relationships between science, literature, and film, from an international and interdisciplinary perspective.

CMLIT 130: The world of banned books, their history, and their politics, studied comparatively and internationally.
CMLIT 131: Issues of ethics, truth, justice, and social order as embodied in crime and detective literature, presented in comparative contexts.
CMLIT 132: Introduction to Nobel Prize winning literature and the culture of the prize in international and historical context.

CMLIT 153: Comparison of narrative techniques employed by literature and film in portraying different cultures, topics may vary each semester.
CMLIT 183Q: In this honors course, we'll explore changing perspectives on life and approaches to studying life.
CMLIT 184: This course is designed to introduce students to the art of the short story and to acquaint them with some of its most talented writers.
CMLIT 185: Development of the modern novel in the last century (outside the British Isles and the United States); lectures, discussions, readings in translation.
